conversation.task: This is a fictional, low-stakes paper-game rehearsal. A hobby club has twenty minutes, twelve blank cards, scrap paper, and pencils to draft one playable three-card game. A teammate says the first draft is confusing and proposes putting twelve rule slogans on a single small card. You think that card will be hard to read. One imagined participant says a fast verbal explanation leaves them behind and asks for a written example. The group can try either matching pairs or sorting cards by drawn shapes; both are reversible paper prototypes. The known downside is that trying a second prototype uses five of the twenty minutes. There is no evidence about which game the group prefers. Nobody has proposed a process. Reply in English in no more than 250 words. Include a short welcoming opening, your response to the proposal and concern, a comparison of feasible approaches with one usable example, and a usable plan for this bounded session. Treat all advice as provisional for the fictional group to choose; do not execute anything.
conversation.response:
Welcome—here’s a concrete starting example the group could choose: draw a circle on two cards and a triangle on the third. Lay all three face up. A player points to the two cards with identical shapes; a correct match earns one point and ends the round. Written example: “○ △ ○ → choose the first and third cards.” Players can take turns across rounds, shuffling between rounds.

I agree that the confusing draft needs clarification. Twelve slogans on one small card could be hard to read and may introduce more ambiguity. Could we instead put a short rule and a worked example on scrap paper beside the three playing cards? That would also answer the request for written support; participants could read at their own pace before asking questions.

Two feasible options are:

- **Matching pairs:** use the example above. It needs little explanation, although the visible match may offer limited challenge.
- **Sorting shapes:** draw one circle, triangle, and square; write the target order “circle → triangle → square” on scrap paper. Players arrange the shuffled cards to match it. This is also simple but requires an agreed ordering.

A provisional twenty-minute plan: spend two minutes choosing together, four drafting cards and written instructions, five trying the game, five revising—or testing the alternative—and four checking and recording the final rules. Testing the alternative costs those five minutes of revision time. There’s no evidence of a preferred game, so invite disagreement and let the group decide.
